content.p: SCHEDULE
FURTHER AMENDMENTS OF THE CRIMES ACT 1914

p.b: An Act to amend certain Acts in relation to criminal and law enforcement matters, and for related purposes

content.p: [Assented to 23 August 1991]
The Parliament of Australia enacts:
1. This Act may be cited as the Crimes Legislation Amendment Act (No. 2) 1991.
2. (1) Subject to this section, this Act commences on the day on which it receives the Royal Assent.
(2) Sections 5 to 10 (inclusive), Parts 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9 and sections 40 to 50 (inclusive) commence 28 days after the day on which this Act receives the Royal Assent.

item.p: Subject to subsections (4) and (5), section 51 and Part 8 commence on a day or days to be fixed by Proclamation.

If the commencement of Part 8 is not fixed by a Proclamation published in the Gazette within the period of 6 months beginning on the day on which this Act receives the Royal Assent, the Part is repealed on the first day after the end of that period.

If section 51 does not commence under subsection (3) within the period of 6 months beginning on the day on which this Act receives the Royal Assent, it commences on the first day after the end of that period.

part.heading: AMENDMENTS OF THE AUSTRALIAN FEDERAL POLICE ACT 1979

section.heading: Notice of application for restraining order

content.p: 8. After section 49e of the Principal Act the following section is inserted:

“(2) Subsections 49d (1), (2), (3) and (5) apply, with the necessary changes made, to the extension of the period of operation of a restraining order made in reliance on subsection 49e (2) in the same way as they apply to the making of a restraining order.
“(3) The DPP must give written notice of an application under subsection (1) for the extension of a restraining order to:

item.p: the owner of the property against which the restraining order was made; and

content.p: 9. The amendments made by sections 7 and 8 do not apply to an application made under subsection 49e (3) of the Principal Act before the commencement of this section.
10. (1) Section 49j of the Principal Act is amended by omitting paragraph (1) (c) and substituting the following paragraph:
“(c) an order for the examination on oath before the court or the Registrar of the court of any person, including:

(ii) the defendant;
about the affairs (including the nature and location of any property) of:

part.heading: AMENDMENTS OF THE CASH TRANSACTION REPORTS ACT 1988

content.p: 11. In this Part, “Principal Act” means the Cash Transaction Reports Act 19882.
12. Section 16 of the Principal Act is amended:
(a) by omitting from subsection (5) everything after “in relation to” and substituting:
“any action by the cash dealer or person taken:

item.p: under this section; or
in the mistaken belief that such action was required under this section.”;

content.p: (b) by inserting after subsection (5) the following subsections:

“(5a) Where a cash dealer communicates to the Director, under subsection (1), information about the cash dealer’s suspicion in relation to a transaction to which the cash dealer is a party, the cash dealer must not, unless required to do so under this Act or any other Act, disclose to anyone else:

item.p: that the cash dealer has formed the suspicion; or
that information has been communicated to the Director; or

any other information from which the person to whom the information is disclosed could reasonably be expected to infer that the suspicion had been formed or that the first-mentioned information had been communicated.

content.p: “(5b) A cash dealer who contravenes subsection (5a) is guilty of an offence punishable on conviction by a fine not exceeding $5,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding 2 years, or both.
“(5c) Subsection (5a) does not prevent a cash dealer from communicating or disclosing to any court any information, or matter, referred to in that subsection.”.
13. After section 17 of the Principal Act, the following section is inserted in Part II:

“17a. (1) The Director may, by written notice to a cash dealer, require the dealer to give the authorised officer specified in the notice access to the dealer’s premises so specified on the day and during the hours so specified.
“(2) The hours specified in a notice must occur during the cash dealer’s normal business hours.
“(3) A cash dealer must comply with a notice.

“(4) Where an authorised officer is given access to premises under a notice, the officer may, for the purposes of monitoring the cash dealer’s compliance with section 16, inspect any system that may be used by the dealer at those premises for identifying and recording transactions that are, or might be, covered by subsection 16 (1) and any records that’ may be kept on, or may be accessible from, the premises relating to such transactions.”.

item.p: In this Part, “Principal Act” means the Crimes Act 19143.
After section 21f of the Principal Act the following sections are inserted in Division 10 of Part 1b:

p.b: Conditions etc. that a court may impose on certain offenders

content.p: “22. (1) Where a court makes a relevant order or passes a relevant sentence in respect of a person charged with, or convicted of:

item.p: an offence against a law of the Commonwealth or of a Territory, being an offence that is a serious narcotics offence; or
a prescribed offence against a law of the Commonwealth or of a Territory;

content.p: it may, at the same time or at a later time, order the person to do all or any of the following things:

item.p: to remain in Australia;
to refrain from applying for, or obtaining, an Australian passport;
to surrender possession of any Australian passport held by the person.

content.p: “(2) Subject to subsection (3), an order made under subsection (1) has effect during such reasonable period as is specified by the court in the order.
“(3) The court may, by order, revoke an order made under subsection (1) or vary such an order as the court sees fit.

“(4) If the court makes an order under subsection (1) or (3), the Registrar or other appropriate officer of the court, as the case requires, must, as soon as practicable, give to the Secretary to the Department administering the Passports Act 1938 a copy of the order.
“(5) If the court makes an order under paragraph (1) (e):

item.p: the passport must be given to the Registrar or other appropriate officer of the court; and
the Registrar or officer must cause the passport to be kept in such custody as he or she thinks fit until:

content.p: (i) the passport is required to be released under subsection (6); or
(ii) the passport is cancelled or expires;
whichever happens first.

“(6) If a passport surrendered under an order under paragraph (1) (e) is in force when that order ceases to have effect, the person having the custody of the passport at that time must, on the application of the person to whom it was issued, cause it to be returned to that person.
“(7) In this section:
‘relevant order’ means an order:

item.p: remanding a person, whether on bail or in custody; or
suspending the sentence passed on a person upon his or her entering into a recognizance; or

content.p: (c) releasing the person on conditions under subsection 20 (1);
‘relevant sentence’ means:

item.p: a sentence of imprisonment other than a suspended sentence; or
a sentence under section 20ab;

content.p: ‘serious narcotics offence’ has the same meaning as in section 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 1987.
“22a. (1) If, under a law of a State, a court makes an order requiring a person charged with, or convicted of:

item.p: a serious narcotics offence against a law of that State; or
such other serious offence against a law of that State as is specified in the first-mentioned law;

content.p: to surrender possession of any Australian passport held by the person, the person must surrender the passport to the Registrar, or other appropriate officer, of the court to be dealt with in accordance with that law.
“(2) In this section:
‘serious narcotics offence’ has the same meaning as in section 7 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 1987”.

p.b: When restraining order ceases to be in force

content.p: 49. (1) Section 57 of the Principal Act is amended:

item.p: by inserting in subparagraph (2) (e) (i) “that is a pecuniary penalty order” after “confiscation order”;
by omitting from subparagraph (2) (e) (ii) “confiscation order” and substituting “pecuniary penalty order”;

by omitting from paragraph (2) (e) “when the confiscation order is satisfied or otherwise ceases to be in force” and substituting “, upon the pecuniary penalty order being satisfied or otherwise ceasing to be in force, to the extent that the property to which the restraining order relates is the same as the property that is sold or otherwise disposed of to satisfy the pecuniary penalty order and pay the costs, charges, expenses and remuneration referred to in subsection 49 (6)”;
by inserting in paragraph (2) (g) “19 or” after “section”.

content.p: (2) The amendments made by subsection (1) apply in relation to restraining orders made before or after the commencement of this section.
50. Section 66 of the Principal Act is amended:

item.p: by omitting from paragraph (1) (d) “and”;
by omitting paragraph (e).

section.heading: State and Territory courts to have jurisdiction

content.p: 51. Section 98 of the Principal Act is amended:

item.p: by omitting from subsection (2) “subsections (3) and (5)” and substituting “this section”;
by omitting subsection (3) and substituting the following subsections:

content.p: “(3) A court cannot make a forfeiture order in respect of property if the court does not have jurisdiction with respect to the recovery of property of that kind.

“(3a) A court may make a forfeiture order in respect of property even though, apart from this section, the court does not have jurisdiction with respect to property whose value equals the value of that property.”;
(c) by omitting subsection (5) and substituting the following subsections:
“(5) Where:

item.p: a court makes a pecuniary penalty order of a particular amount; and

the court does not have jurisdiction with respect to the recovery of debts of an amount equal to that amount, the registrar of the court must issue a certificate containing the prescribed particulars.

content.p: “(5a) The certificate may be registered, in accordance with the regulations, in a court having jurisdiction with respect to the recovery of debts of an amount equal to the amount of the pecuniary penalty order.
“(5b) Upon registration in a court, the certificate is enforceable in all respects as a final judgment of the court in favour of the Commonwealth.”.
SCHEDULE Section 22
FURTHER AMENDMENTS OF THE CRIMES ACT 1914
Insert:

“ ‘aggregate’, in relation to 2 or more sentences or terms of imprisonment, or in relation to the unserved portions of such sentences or terms, means the total effective sentence or term of imprisonment imposed, or remaining unserved, as the case may be, having regard to whether the sentences or terms are to be served cumulatively, partly cumulatively or concurrently.
The aggregate of 3 sentences, each of 2 years, to be served concurrently, is 2 years.
The aggregate of 3 sentences, each of 2 years, where 2 sentences are to be served concurrently and one is to be served cumulatively, is 4 years.

The aggregate of a one year unserved portion of a sentence, a 2 year unserved portion of another sentence, to be served concurrently with the first sentence, and a 2 year sentence to be served cumulatively, is 4 years.
After “because” insert “of.
EXAMPLES DEMONSTRATING MEANING OF “AGGREGATE”

item.p: Omit “must, by order, direct when each federal sentence imposed by it for the first-mentioned offence commences, but so that:”, substitute “must, when imposing a federal sentence for that federal offence, or for each of those federal offences, by order direct when the federal sentence commences, but so that:”.
Omit “each federal sentence does not commence”, substitute “no federal sentence commences”.

content.p: Omit “each federal sentence does not commence”, substitute “no federal sentence commences”.
Repeal sections 19ab, 19ac, 19ad and 19ae, substitute:

p.b: When court must fix non-parole period or make a recognizance release order

content.p: “19ab. (1) Subject to subsection (3), where:
(a) a person is convicted of a federal offence, or of 2 or more federal offences at the same sitting; and
SCHEDULE—continued

item.p: a court imposes on the person a federal life sentence, or a federal sentence that exceeds, or federal sentences that, in the aggregate, exceed 3 years; and
at the time the sentence or sentences are imposed, the person is not already serving or subject to a federal sentence;

content.p: the court must either:

item.p: fix a single non-parole period in respect of that sentence or those sentences; or
make a recognizance release order.

content.p: “(2) Subject to subsection (3), where:

item.p: while a person is in prison and is serving or subject to a federal sentence, a further federal sentence is imposed on the person; and
the result is that the person is to serve or to complete a federal life sentence or federal sentences the unserved portions of which, in the aggregate, exceed 3 years; and
at the time the further federal sentence is imposed, the person is not already subject to a non-parole period or recognizance release order in respect of a federal sentence;

content.p: the court imposing the further sentence must either:

item.p: fix a single non-parole period in respect of all federal sentences the person is to serve or complete; or
make a recognizance release order.

content.p: “(3) Where, but for this subsection, a court would be required by this section to fix a non-parole period, or make a recognizance release order, in respect of a person, the court may decline to do either if, having regard to the nature and circumstances of the offence or offences concerned and to the antecedents of the person, the court is satisfied that neither is appropriate.
“(4) Where the court decides that neither a non-parole period nor a recognizance release order is appropriate, the court must:

item.p: state its reasons for so deciding; and
cause the reasons to be entered in the records of the court.

p.b: When court must fix a recognizance release order

content.p: “19ac. (1) Subject to subsections (3) and (4), where:

item.p: a person is convicted of a federal offence, or of 2 or more federal offences at the same sitting; and
the court imposes on the person a federal sentence that does not exceed, or federal sentences that, in the aggregate, do not exceed, 3 years; and
at the time the sentence or sentences are imposed the person is not already serving or subject to a federal sentence;

content.p: SCHEDULE—continued
the court must make a recognizance release order in respect of that sentence or those sentences and must not fix a non-parole period.
“(2) Subject to subsections (3) and (4), where:

item.p: while a person is in prison and is serving or subject to a federal sentence, a further federal sentence is imposed on the person; and
the result is that the person is to serve or to complete federal sentences the unserved portions of which do not exceed, in the aggregate, 3 years; and
at the time the further federal sentence is imposed, the person is not already subject to a recognizance release order in respect of a federal sentence;

content.p: the court imposing the further sentence must make a recognizance release order in respect of all federal sentences to be served or completed by the person and must not fix a non-parole period.
“(3) Where:

item.p: the federal sentence or federal sentences referred to in paragraph (1) (b); or
the unserved portions of the federal sentences referred to in paragraph (2) (b);

content.p: in the aggregate, do not exceed 6 months, the court is not required to make a recognizance release order.

“(4) Where, but for this subsection, a court would be required by this section to make a recognizance release order in respect of a person, the court may decline to do so if, having regard to the nature and circumstances of the offence or offences concerned and to the antecedents of the person, the court is satisfied that such an order is not appropriate.
“(5) Where the court decides that a recognizance release order is not appropriate, the court must:

item.p: state its reasons for so deciding; and
cause the reasons to be entered in the records of the court.

p.b: Persons already subject to a non-parole period

content.p: “19ad. (1) Where:

item.p: a non-parole period (in this section called the ‘existing non-parole period’) has been fixed in respect of a federal sentence or federal sentences; and
while the offender is serving the existing non-parole period, a court imposes a further federal sentence on the person;

content.p: this section applies.
SCHEDULE—continued
“(2) Where this section applies, the court must, after considering the relevant circumstances, including:

item.p: the existing non-parole period; and
the nature and circumstances of the offence or offences concerned; and
the antecedents of the person; do one of the following things:
make an order confirming the existing non-parole period;
fix a new single non-parole period in respect of all federal sentences the person is to serve or complete;
where the court decides that, in the circumstances, a non-parole period is not appropriate—cancel the existing non-parole period and decline to fix a new non-parole period.

content.p: “(3) Where, under paragraph (2) (e), the court fixes a new single non-parole period, it:

item.p: is to be treated as having superceded the existing non-parole period; and
must not be such as to allow the person to be released on parole earlier then would have been the case if the further sentence had not been imposed.

content.p: “(4) Where this section applies, the court must not make a recognizance release order.
“(5) Where, under paragraph (2) (f), the court declines to fix a new non-parole period, the court must:

item.p: state its reasons for deciding that a non-parole period is not appropriate; and
cause the reasons to be entered in the records of the court.

p.b: Persons already subject to recognizance release order

content.p: “19ae. (1) Where:

item.p: a person is subject to a recognizance release order (in this section called the ‘existing recognizance release order’) made in respect of a federal sentence or federal sentences; and
before the person is released under that order, the court imposes a further federal sentence on the person;

content.p: this section applies.
“(2) Where this section applies, the court must, after considering the relevant circumstances, including:

item.p: the existing recognizance release order; and
the nature and circumstances of the offence or offences concerned; and

content.p: SCHEDULE—continued
(c) the antecedents of the person;
do one of the following things:

item.p: make an order confirming the existing recognizance release order;
make a new recognizance release order in respect of all federal sentences the person is to serve or complete;

where, as a result of the further federal sentence being imposed, the person is to serve or to complete a federal life sentence or federal sentences the unserved portions of which, in the aggregate, exceed 3 years and the court decides that it is appropriate to fix a non-parole period—fix a single non-parole period in respect of all federal sentences the person is to serve or complete;

where the court decides that, in the circumstances, neither a recognizance release order nor a non-parole period is appropriate—cancel the existing recognizance release order and decline to make a new recognizance release order.

content.p: “(3) Where, under paragraph (2) (e), the court makes a new recognizance release order, that order:

item.p: is to be treated as having superceded the existing recognizance release order; and
must not be such as to allow the person to be released earlier than would have been the case if the further sentence had not been imposed.

content.p: “(4) Where, under paragraph (2) (f), the court fixes a single non-parole period, it:

item.p: is to be treated as having superceded the existing recognizance release order; and
must not be such as to allow the person to be released on parole earlier than he or she would have been released if the further sentence had not been imposed.

content.p: “(5) Where, under paragraph (2) (g), the court declines to make a new recognizance release order, the court must:

item.p: state its reasons for deciding that neither a recognizance release order nor a non-parole period is appropriate; and
cause the reasons to be entered in the records of the court.”.
